suggestions.rationale: Paclitaxel-containing chemotherapy used to treat ovarian cancer can produce clinically significant peripheral sensory neuropathy. In the randomized MITO-7 phase 3 ovarian-cancer trial, grade 2 or worse neuropathy occurred in both carboplatin-plus-paclitaxel schedules, with a lower frequency in the weekly schedule than the every-three-weeks schedule. This supports a treatment-complication pathway only when the individual received a documented neurotoxic ovarian-cancer regimen and a compatible peripheral neuropathy began or materially worsened afterward; ovarian cancer itself, surgery alone, or a non-neurotoxic treatment history should not be treated as sufficient evidence of causation.

pathwayIntelligence.causalChain: Ovarian cancer → documented paclitaxel-containing chemotherapy, if administered → neurotoxic treatment exposure → clinically confirmed peripheral neuropathy with compatible timing and phenotype.
developmentQuestions: Which ovarian-cancer chemotherapy agents, doses, schedules, and cumulative exposures were actually administered?
Did numbness, tingling, neuropathic pain, sensory loss, weakness, or gait symptoms begin or materially worsen after the neurotoxic treatment exposure?
What neurologic examination, electrodiagnostic testing, or other clinical assessment supports peripheral neuropathy and its phenotype?
Did symptoms improve, persist, or progress with dose modification, treatment completion, or discontinuation?

Which competing causes, including diabetes, alcohol exposure, nutritional deficiency, thyroid disease, renal disease, other neurotoxic drugs, entrapment neuropathy, or pre-existing neuropathy, should be addressed?
issuesToResolve: The evidence is treatment-specific and should not be generalized from ovarian cancer to peripheral neuropathy without documented paclitaxel or another clinically supported neurotoxic exposure.
Neuropathy is multifactorial; chronology, phenotype, cumulative treatment exposure, and alternative causes require individual review.

evidenceGaps: Oncology records identifying the exact chemotherapy regimen, dose, schedule, and cumulative exposure
Documentation of neuropathy onset, course, severity, and treatment-response chronology
Neurologic examination and electrodiagnostic testing when clinically indicated
Assessment of competing causes of peripheral neuropathy

sourceReferences.citation: Pignata S, Scambia G, Katsaros D, et al. Carboplatin plus paclitaxel once a week versus every 3 weeks in patients with advanced ovarian cancer (MITO-7): a randomised, multicentre, open-label, phase 3 trial. Lancet Oncol. 2014;15(4):396-405. PMID 24582486
sourceReferences.note: Randomized phase 3 trial of 810 eligible women with ovarian cancer receiving carboplatin plus paclitaxel reported grade 2 or worse neuropathy in 6% of the weekly-treatment group and 17% of the every-three-weeks group. Supports a paclitaxel-containing-treatment complication pathway, not neuropathy attribution from ovarian cancer itself.

suggestions.rationale: Mapping Expansion Batch ME-6 adds this relationship only as a bounded clinical proposition. Require documented ovarian cancer, documented pelvic and/or para-aortic lymph-node dissection or lymphadenectomy, and separately established lower-extremity lymphedema with compatible postoperative chronology. Do not infer lymphedema from ovarian cancer, chemotherapy, or pelvic surgery without lymphatic-node disruption alone. Preserve venous thrombosis or insufficiency, obesity, infection, cardiac or renal edema, prior pelvic surgery or radiotherapy, malignant obstruction, and other causes of lower-extremity swelling. The cited literature supports only this constrained relationship and does not, by itself, establish an individual medical nexus.
evidenceGaps: Independent documentation of ovarian-cancer and lymphedema
Documentation satisfying the approved phenotype restriction: lower-extremity lymphedema after lymph-node dissection
Chronology and phenotype compatible with the bounded source proposition
Assessment of competing etiologies, shared risk factors, and treatment effects where applicable
